strengths: Clear and interesting central finding: L0 is not a free hyperparameter but has a 'correct' value determined by the true sparsity of underlying features, and deviating from it (in either direction) causes feature mixing/degeneracy. This challenges the common 'sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff' framing used broadly in the SAE literature.

The toy model experiments (Section 3, Figure 1, Appendix A.2/A.3) are well controlled with known ground truth, clearly demonstrating that low L0 causes correlated-feature mixing and that MSE actively rewards this incorrect solution over the ground-truth dictionary — a compelling and clean illustration of the core claim.

The proposed N-th decoder projection metric (s^dec_n) is a novel, simple, unsupervised diagnostic that requires no ground truth and is shown to be robust to choice of N in both toy and LLM settings (Figures 2, 3, 10).

The LLM validation on Gemma-2-2b connects the toy-model metric to a real downstream task (sparse probing F1), showing the metric's optimum coincides with peak probing performance (Figure 4), lending some external validity to the approach.

Practically relevant finding: survey of open-source SAEs on Neuronpedia (Appendix A.5) shows most public SAEs use L0 well below what the paper's analysis suggests is optimal, which if correct has significant implications for the community.

Honest and fairly detailed limitations section and inclusion of a preliminary automatic L0-tuning procedure (Appendix A.4) with discussion of its practical difficulties, showing methodological transparency.
weaknesses: The LLM-scale claim that 'true L0' is 200-250 rests entirely on a single model/layer (Gemma-2-2b, layer 12) and a single training distribution (The Pile), yet the paper generalizes broadly ('most SAEs used by researchers have L0 too low'); this is a substantial overreach given the narrow empirical base (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation, but the abstract/discussion still make strong general claims).

The core validation of 'correctness' on LLMs is indirect: there is no ground truth for true L0 in Gemma-2-2b, so the paper relies on (a) its own proposed metric and (b) sparse probing F1, which is itself a proxy with known caveats (probing performance need not equal correct disentangled feature recovery, especially since increasing L0 could simply give probes more capacity/parameters, akin to giving a probe more directions to work with regardless of feature correctness).

The toy model itself is fairly simple (50 orthogonal features, fixed correlation structure, single firing-magnitude distribution) and may not capture more complex phenomena like hierarchical/compositional features, feature splitting/absorption, or high-dimensional superposition regimes relevant to real LLMs — the mapping from toy model conclusions to LLM behavior is asserted rather than rigorously established.

No statistical uncertainty or repeated-seed analysis is reported; single-run toy model and single-run LLM sweep results are presented as if definitive, without error bars or robustness checks across random seeds, correlation matrices, or different layers/models.

The paper only studies BatchTopK SAEs (Appendix A.6 limitations acknowledges this) while claiming (without evidence) that findings generalize to L1/JumpReLU SAEs; this is an unverified extrapolation given these architectures set sparsity indirectly via loss coefficients and may behave differently.

The s^dec_n metric's practical utility for a practitioner is limited: the automatic L0-tuning procedure in Appendix A.4 is described as requiring heavy hyperparameter tuning and did not work robustly for LLMs, undermining the paper's practical actionability despite the strong prescriptive claims in the abstract ('practitioners must set L0 correctly').

The paper is quite short (4 main pages) with limited related work discussion and no comparison against alternative methods for choosing L0 (e.g., simple validation-based downstream task tuning, other proposed sparsity-selection heuristics), making it hard to assess the added value of s^dec_n over simpler baselines.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: code availability is mentioned but the repository link appears missing/empty in the text ('Our code is available at' with no URL), and specifics of correlation matrix generation, exact hyperparameters for LLM SAE training beyond learning rate, and compute budget are only partly specified.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important question: whether L0 is a truly free hyperparameter for SAEs, challenging the common 'sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff' framing used throughout the SAE literature.

Toy model experiments are clean and compelling: with known ground-truth orthogonal features and controlled correlation structures, the paper convincingly shows that SAEs at incorrect L0 (too low or too high) mix correlated/anti-correlated features into latents, while the correct L0 recovers ground truth exactly.

The demonstration that a perfect ground-truth SAE can score *worse* on reconstruction than an incorrect, feature-mixing SAE (Fig. 4-5) is a striking and important result that undermines a widely used evaluation practice in the field.

The proposed n-th decoder projection metric (s_dec_n) is intuitive, cheap to compute, and is validated in both toy models (matching true L0 exactly) and two real LLMs (Gemma-2-2b, Llama-3.2-1b), where its 'elbow' roughly coincides with peak sparse-probing performance.

Extensive supplementary analysis (alternative cosine-similarity metric, JumpReLU vs BatchTopK threshold/bias dynamics, L0 audit of open-source Neuronpedia SAEs, L0-transition training experiments) adds robustness and practical relevance, and the audit showing most public SAEs use too-low L0 has direct actionable value for the community.
Limitations and negative results (e.g., automatic L0-tuning via gradient estimation working in toy models but not robustly in LLMs) are reported honestly rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The LLM validation of the central claim relies on indirect proxies (elbow location of s_dec_n roughly matching peak sparse-probing F1) rather than any ground-truth notion of 'correct' features in real models, so the core toy-model finding is not rigorously confirmed at scale; it is essentially a correlational, not causal, validation.

The metric requires choosing n (e.g., near h/2), and the paper acknowledges this choice is largely empirical/heuristic with inconsistent behavior at high L0 across settings (sometimes a clear minimum, sometimes a shallow plateau), limiting its reliability as a general diagnostic tool.

Experiments are limited to a small number of models/layers (essentially one layer each in Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.2-1b, plus one cross-architecture comparison at layer 12), and the toy models use fairly simple correlation structures (single correlated hub feature, or one random correlation matrix), so generalization to more complex/realistic feature geometries and other layers/models is not well established.

Several explanations for observed phenomena (e.g., why JumpReLU handles high L0 better than BatchTopK, why encoder bias/threshold trends differ) are speculative ('we suspect') and not tested with targeted causal experiments beyond post-hoc correlational plots.

The proposed automatic L0-tuning procedure (Appendix A.6) is reported to work poorly and require heavy hyperparameter tuning on real LLMs, so the paper's practical contribution is currently limited to a diagnostic requiring a manual L0 sweep, which is expensive.
Limited statistical rigor (3-5 seeds), and the paper does not compare against other plausible baselines/heuristics for choosing L0 beyond its own two proposed metrics.
The code availability link is left incomplete ('Code is available at'), raising minor reproducibility concerns.
